title: Gallbladder Disease: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, Cholangitis, or Pancreatitis?
bottomLine: Gallstone disease is managed by syndrome, not by the presence of stones alone. Distinguish uncomplicated biliary colic from acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis/cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis because infection, obstruction and organ dysfunction change urgency and procedure needs.
recognize: Biliary colic causes episodic postprandial RUQ/epigastric pain without persistent systemic inflammation.
Persistent pain, fever and focal RUQ tenderness support cholecystitis; jaundice/cholestatic labs raise common-duct obstruction; cholangitis adds systemic infection.
differentiate: Incidental asymptomatic gallstones do not automatically require treatment.
Pancreatitis, peptic ulcer, hepatitis and cardiac disease can mimic upper abdominal pain.
assessment: Assess pain duration, fever, vomiting, jaundice, hemodynamics, pregnancy and prior gallstone/pancreatitis episodes.
workup: Use CBC/liver chemistry/lipase as indicated and RUQ ultrasound as first-line imaging for suspected gallbladder disease.
Further ductal imaging/intervention depends on obstruction probability and local specialty pathway.
management: Uncomplicated biliary colic needs symptom control and surgical follow-up when appropriate.
Acute cholecystitis requires antibiotics/surgical pathway; cholangitis requires urgent antibiotics plus biliary decompression/source control.
Gallstone pancreatitis is managed by pancreatitis severity plus biliary indication.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antibiotics for uncomplicated biliary colic.
Pregnancy and renal/GI risk alter analgesic selection.
counselling: Explain that stones matter when they cause symptoms, inflammation or obstruction—not simply because imaging found them.
followUp: Close the loop on surgical/GI referral and recurrent symptoms.
examTrap: Treating incidental gallstones with antibiotics or calling jaundice-plus-fever simple biliary colic.
oneLinePearl: Gallstones are the substrate; infection and obstruction determine urgency.
sourceBasis: Canadian hepatobiliary and acute-care practice principles

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Average-Risk Screening Is Not Symptom Workup
bottomLine: Colorectal screening is for asymptomatic people. Use the current provincial or territorial average-risk program and family-history pathway; rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, unexplained weight loss or persistent bowel-habit change requires diagnostic evaluation rather than a screening FIT.
recognize: Average-risk eligibility and funded intervals can differ by province/territory and can change over time.
Prior adenoma, IBD, hereditary syndrome or strong family history moves a patient outside ordinary average-risk screening.
differentiate: FIT detects occult blood for screening; it is not a diagnostic rule-out test for symptomatic disease.
Post-polypectomy surveillance and hereditary-risk colonoscopy are not the same as population screening.
assessment: Clarify whether the patient is truly asymptomatic, then review family history, prior polyps/cancer, IBD, prior screening and ability to complete follow-up.
workup: Use the jurisdiction's current FIT/colonoscopy pathway for eligible asymptomatic patients.
Use diagnostic colonoscopy or other evaluation based on symptoms/alarm features rather than sending a symptomatic patient through routine screening.
management: Offer evidence-supported screening and ensure abnormal screening results receive timely diagnostic colonoscopy.
Use surveillance intervals based on prior colonoscopy/pathology quality and current specialist guidance.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet management around colonoscopy/polypectomy is procedure- and indication-specific; do not stop therapy reflexively.
counselling: Explain the difference between screening and diagnostic testing and why an abnormal FIT is not itself a cancer diagnosis.
followUp: Track every abnormal screen until definitive diagnostic resolution and document the next surveillance interval.
examTrap: Ordering FIT for a patient with rectal bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia instead of starting a diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Provincial and territorial colorectal screening programs

title: Chronic Diarrhea: Classify the Pattern Before Ordering Everything
bottomLine: Chronic diarrhea is a syndrome. Separate watery, fatty/malabsorptive and inflammatory patterns, review medications and travel/exposure, and use targeted celiac, inflammatory, infection, thyroid, bile-acid or endoscopic testing based on the phenotype rather than ordering a broad indiscriminate panel.
recognize: Nocturnal diarrhea, blood, anemia, weight loss, fever or elevated inflammatory markers raise concern for organic disease.
Medication-induced diarrhea is common and often missed.
differentiate: IBS-D is a positive diagnosis without objective inflammatory alarm features.
Bile-acid diarrhea, celiac disease, microscopic colitis, IBD, chronic infection and pancreatic insufficiency can overlap clinically.
assessment: Characterize duration, nocturnal symptoms, blood/fat, frequency/volume, weight, travel, diet, surgery, medication, immune status and family history.
workup: Use CBC/chemistry, celiac serology, inflammatory markers/calprotectin, stool testing or colonoscopy selectively based on the pattern.
Consider bile-acid diarrhea in the appropriate chronic watery phenotype rather than labeling refractory symptoms IBS automatically.
management: Treat the identified cause, restore hydration/nutrition and stop contributing medications when safe.
Use symptom-directed therapy only after dangerous/inflammatory/infectious causes are reasonably addressed.
medicationSafety: Avoid antimotility agents in severe inflammatory/toxic diarrhea or suspected invasive infection until appropriately assessed.
counselling: Explain why targeted testing is more useful than repeated broad stool/lab panels.
followUp: Reassess unresolved symptoms and close loops on endoscopy/biopsy results.
examTrap: Calling months of nocturnal bloody diarrhea IBS because the patient also has stress-related symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Classify chronic diarrhea first; the pattern determines the test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology guideline library including bile-acid diarrhea

title: GI Bleeding: Stabilize First, Localize Second
bottomLine: GI bleeding is a hemodynamic problem before it is an endoscopic diagnosis. Assess airway/perfusion, establish IV access, trend hemoglobin in context, manage anticoagulant/antiplatelet issues, use restrictive transfusion principles in stable patients, and obtain urgent endoscopic/interventional care according to bleeding source and severity.
recognize: Hematemesis/melena suggests upper bleeding but brisk upper bleeding can present with hematochezia.
Early hemoglobin can be deceptively normal before equilibration; shock signs and ongoing bleeding matter more than one initial value.
differentiate: Iron-deficiency anemia/occult loss is different from active unstable hemorrhage.
Variceal bleeding requires portal-hypertension-specific acute therapy in addition to general resuscitation.
assessment: Assess ABCs, orthostasis/hemodynamics, ongoing bleeding, syncope, liver disease, NSAIDs, anticoagulants/antiplatelets and prior GI disease.
workup: Use CBC, coagulation, renal/liver chemistry, type/screen and cause-directed imaging/endoscopy.
Do not use fecal occult blood testing to 'confirm' clinically obvious or symptomatic GI bleeding.
management: Resuscitate, correct severe coagulopathy/reversal only when clinically indicated, and arrange endoscopy/intervention based on source and stability.
Use PPI therapy for suspected upper nonvariceal bleeding and variceal-specific therapy when portal-hypertension bleeding is suspected.
medicationSafety: Balance thrombosis and bleeding risk when holding/reversing antithrombotic therapy; restart planning is part of care.
Avoid unnecessary transfusion in stable patients while never delaying blood in hemorrhagic shock.
counselling: After stabilization, review NSAID/alcohol/medication contributors and clear rebleeding precautions.
followUp: Ensure pathology/endoscopy results, antithrombotic restart and cause-specific prevention are closed-loop.
examTrap: Using a normal initial hemoglobin to rule out a major acute GI bleed.
oneLinePearl: In GI bleeding, the blood pressure and perfusion outrank the first hemoglobin.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology GI bleeding/endoscopy guidance

title: Abdominal Pain: Disposition Before Diagnostic Perfection
bottomLine: Abdominal pain is a disposition problem before it is a final-diagnosis problem. Identify shock, peritonitis, pregnancy emergencies, ischemia, obstruction, perforation, GI bleeding and other time-sensitive causes first, while treating pain and using targeted labs/imaging based on the differential.
recognize: Peritonitis, pain out of proportion, persistent bilious/feculent vomiting, significant bleeding and hemodynamic instability are high-risk findings.
Older/immunocompromised patients can have muted fever/tenderness despite serious disease.
differentiate: Cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, vascular, GU and gynecologic disease can present as abdominal pain.
A normal early lab panel does not exclude ischemia, appendicitis or ectopic pregnancy.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, onset/location/migration, vomiting/stool/urine, bleeding, fever, prior surgery, medications and pregnancy possibility.
Perform focused abdominal plus relevant pelvic/testicular/cardiopulmonary exam.
workup: Use pregnancy testing, CBC/chemistry, liver/pancreatic tests, urinalysis, ECG/troponin and imaging only as guided by the differential.
Choose ultrasound when it answers the question without unnecessary radiation.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetics while evaluating; appropriate analgesia does not prevent diagnosis.
Escalate suspected peritonitis, ischemia, perforation, compromised obstruction, ectopic pregnancy or shock urgently.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen GI bleeding/renal disease; opioids require sedation/respiratory monitoring but should not be withheld when severe pain warrants appropriate treatment.
counselling: For safe outpatient care, give explicit return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding or syncope.
followUp: Reassess unresolved pain and pending imaging/lab results until a stable endpoint is reached.
examTrap: Withholding analgesia or ordering every abdominal test before deciding whether the patient is unstable.
oneLinePearl: Stabilize and identify the surgical patient before chasing a perfect label.

title: Liver Test Interpretation in GI Disease: Injury, Cholestasis, and Function Are Different
bottomLine: Interpret liver tests by pattern and clinical context. AST/ALT reflect injury, alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin help define cholestasis/handling, and INR/albumin provide different information about synthetic function; falling aminotransferases are not reassuring if INR, bilirubin, glucose or mental status are worsening.
recognize: Hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns guide different differentials and imaging needs.
ALP can be bone/placental as well as hepatic; albumin is influenced by inflammation/nutrition/renal loss.
differentiate: High aminotransferases do not equal liver failure.
A normal ALT does not exclude cirrhosis or MASLD fibrosis.
assessment: Assess jaundice, pruritus, pain, fever, alcohol/medications/supplements, hemodynamics, pregnancy and encephalopathy/bleeding.
workup: Classify the biochemical pattern, then order cause-directed viral, toxic, autoimmune, metabolic and ultrasound/imaging studies.
Assess INR/glucose/mental status in severe acute injury rather than following enzymes alone.
management: Treat cause and severity simultaneously and escalate suspected acute liver failure or obstructive sepsis urgently.
medicationSafety: Do not stop all medications from one minor enzyme abnormality; assess timing, severity, bilirubin and alternative causes.
counselling: Explain that 'liver tests' measure different processes rather than one overall liver score.
followUp: Trend only the tests that answer the clinical question and complete etiologic/fibrosis evaluation when abnormalities persist.
examTrap: Calling falling AST/ALT recovery while synthetic function worsens.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job: injury, bile flow, and synthetic function.

title: Endoscopy: Scope When the Result Can Change Care
bottomLine: Endoscopy is indicated when symptoms, alarm features, bleeding, screening/surveillance risk or therapeutic need justify an invasive test. Do not scope low-risk stable symptoms simply because endoscopy is definitive; ensure pathology, biopsy, polyp and surveillance recommendations are closed-loop after the procedure.
recognize: Progressive dysphagia, significant GI bleeding/anemia, suspicious imaging and selected surveillance indications are common reasons for endoscopy.
Routine repeat endoscopy without a management-changing indication adds cost/risk without benefit.
differentiate: Screening colonoscopy, diagnostic colonoscopy and post-polypectomy surveillance have different indications.
Upper GI series and capsule/endoscopy studies answer different questions and are not interchangeable.
assessment: Clarify the exact question, alarm features, comorbidity, sedation risk, anticoagulants/antiplatelets and whether biopsy/intervention is anticipated.
workup: Use the least invasive test that answers the clinical question when appropriate; select EGD/colonoscopy/capsule or other endoscopy based on suspected site/pathology.
management: Refer appropriately and ensure bowel-prep/medication/sedation planning.
Act on pathology, polyp and surveillance results rather than treating the procedure as the endpoint.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural antithrombotic management depends on thrombotic risk and procedure bleeding risk.
counselling: Explain why an invasive procedure is or is not expected to change care and review post-procedure warning signs.
followUp: Track pathology and surveillance interval ownership explicitly.
examTrap: Repeating endoscopy for stable low-risk symptoms when prior evaluation is adequate and nothing new would change management.
oneLinePearl: Scope when the answer changes care—and own what happens after the scope.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology guideline/endoscopy library

title: Nutrition Assessment: Diagnose the Deficit Before Prescribing Supplements
bottomLine: Nutrition assessment integrates weight trajectory, intake, GI losses/malabsorption, function, physical findings, disease burden and targeted labs. Do not use albumin as a stand-alone nutrition marker or prescribe broad supplement panels without identifying the likely deficiency, cause, dose and monitoring plan.
recognize: Unintentional weight loss, reduced intake, muscle loss/weakness, malabsorption, chronic diarrhea and high metabolic demand can signal malnutrition risk.
Albumin falls with inflammation and illness and is not specific for nutritional status.
differentiate: Iron, B12, folate and vitamin-D deficiencies have different causes/tests and replacement strategies.
Refeeding risk is a distinct emergency-prone state in severely malnourished patients.
assessment: Measure weight trajectory, intake, swallowing, dentition, food access, GI symptoms, alcohol/substances, medications and functional status.
workup: Use targeted CBC/iron/B12/folate/electrolyte/vitamin testing based on phenotype and risk rather than indiscriminate panels.
management: Treat the cause, provide dietitian support and use oral/enteral/parenteral nutrition according to GI function and severity.
In refeeding risk, restore nutrition cautiously with phosphate/potassium/magnesium/thiamine monitoring per protocol.
medicationSafety: Megadose vitamins/minerals can cause toxicity and interactions.
Iron/calcium and other supplements can alter medication absorption.
counselling: Focus on achievable nutrition goals and food access without moralizing diet.
followUp: Track weight/function, intake and cause-specific laboratory response.
examTrap: Calling a low albumin malnutrition without considering inflammation or prescribing every vitamin test/supplement at once.
oneLinePearl: Nutrition care starts with the cause and the trajectory, not one lab value.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Biochemistry recommendations

title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Replace What the Missing Gut Cannot Absorb
bottomLine: Short bowel syndrome is intestinal failure or malabsorption after substantial bowel loss. Management depends on remaining anatomy and adaptation: maintain hydration/electrolytes, optimize nutrient absorption and diet, use antidiarrheal/acid-suppression or specialized therapy when appropriate, and coordinate intestinal-rehabilitation/parenteral support when oral/enteral intake cannot maintain health.
recognize: High-output diarrhea/ostomy, dehydration, weight loss and micronutrient deficiencies are common.
Ileal loss increases bile-acid/B12 issues; colon continuity changes fluid/energy salvage and stone risk.
differentiate: Ordinary chronic diarrhea does not necessarily imply intestinal failure.
High-output ostomy can cause severe sodium/magnesium depletion even when the patient drinks large amounts of hypotonic fluid.
assessment: Document surgical anatomy, stool/ostomy output, hydration, weight, urine output, medications, kidney stones and nutrition-support history.
workup: Trend electrolytes, magnesium, renal function, micronutrients and nutrition markers according to anatomy/therapy.
Assess liver/bone complications of long-term parenteral nutrition when relevant.
management: Use oral rehydration strategies, diet adapted to anatomy, antidiarrheal/antisecretory therapy and targeted supplements.
Refer parenteral-nutrition-dependent or complex patients to intestinal rehabilitation/nutrition specialty care.
medicationSafety: High pill burden and shortened transit can alter drug absorption; formulations may need review.
Avoid telling high-output patients simply to drink more plain water when sodium losses are driving dehydration.
redFlags: Progressive liver disease on parenteral nutrition
counselling: Teach individualized oral-rehydration and output-monitoring plans and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: Track hydration, renal function, micronutrients, weight and nutrition-support complications.
examTrap: Treating severe high-output short bowel with unlimited hypotonic fluids and no sodium/electrolyte strategy.
oneLinePearl: In short bowel, remaining anatomy predicts what the patient cannot absorb.
sourceBasis: Canadian intestinal rehabilitation/clinical nutrition practice principles
